title: Pediatrics & Geriatrics
summary: The two ends of life as their own medicine: children who compensate until they crash and then crash fast, and older adults whose serious disease arrives without fever, without pain, and without a clear story. Normal values, the age-specific workups, and the syndromes that only exist at these ages.

lessons.title: From newborn to teenager: development and its red flags
lessons.body:
## Why a PA has to know milestones

Development is a vital sign. A child who was walking last month and is not walking now has a neurologic problem until proven otherwise. A 14-month-old who cannot sit is not a slow starter, he is a workup. And the single most useful fact in child abuse recognition is developmental: a baby who cannot roll over cannot fall off a couch.

You do not need to memorize the whole Denver screen. You need the anchors and the deadlines.

## The anchors

| Age | Gross motor | Fine motor / language | Social |
|---|---|---|---|
| `2 mo` | Lifts head when prone | Coos | Social smile |
| `4 mo` | Rolls front to back | Reaches, laughs | Recognizes caregiver |
| `6 mo` | Sits with support, tripod | Transfers object hand to hand, babbles | Stranger awareness starting |
| `9 mo` | Sits alone, crawls, pulls to stand | Immature pincer, `mama` nonspecific | Stranger anxiety |
| `12 mo` | First steps | Mature pincer, 1 to 3 words | Waves, points |
| `18 mo` | Walks well, runs stiffly | 10 to 25 words, feeds self with spoon | Imitates chores |
| `2 y` | Runs, kicks a ball, stairs two feet per step | Two-word phrases, about 50 words, half intelligible to a stranger | Parallel play |
| `3 y` | Tricycle, stairs alternating feet | Three-word sentences, 75 percent intelligible, copies a circle | Takes turns |
| `4 y` | Hops on one foot | Copies a cross, fully intelligible | Cooperative play |
| `5 y` | Skips | Copies a triangle, counts to 10 | Follows rules |

## The deadlines

These are the failures that trigger referral rather than reassurance.

- No social smile by `3 months`
- Not sitting unsupported by `9 months`
- Not walking by `18 months`
- No single words by `18 months`; no two-word phrases by `24 months`
- Hand preference before `12 to 18 months`, which suggests weakness on the other side
- **Any loss of a skill the child already had, at any age**

> **Key:** Regression is never a normal variant. A toddler who had words and stopped, or who walked and stopped, gets a neurology and developmental workup regardless of how well the rest of the exam looks.

## The first weeks

Newborns lose up to `7 to 10 percent` of birth weight in the first week and should be back to birth weight by day `10 to 14`, then gain roughly `20 to 30 g per day`. Breastfed infants feed `8 to 12 times` in 24 hours. By day 5, expect `6 or more` wet diapers a day. Poor feeding, poor weight gain, and fewer wet diapers is a triad that brings a newborn back to the emergency department.

Jaundice is the other newborn constant. **Visible jaundice in the first `24 hours` of life is always pathologic** and usually hemolytic. Physiologic jaundice appears after 24 hours and peaks around day `3 to 5`. Conjugated (direct) bilirubin above `1 mg/dL` or above 20 percent of the total is also always pathologic and raises biliary atresia, which is time-sensitive surgery.

## The adolescent

Adolescence is a different clinical encounter, not just a bigger child. Part of every adolescent visit happens with the parent out of the room, and the structured way to do it is the HEEADSSS interview: Home, Education and employment, Eating, Activities, Drugs, Sexuality, Suicide and depression, Safety.

Confidentiality is what makes honest answers possible, and it has limits you state out loud at the start: you keep what is said private unless someone is going to be hurt, meaning suicidal or homicidal intent or abuse. In **New Jersey** a minor can consent on their own to testing and treatment for sexually transmitted infections, to pregnancy-related care, and to treatment for substance use disorder. Other care generally still needs a parent, and the specifics vary, so confirm against current state law rather than memory.

> **On shift:** Ask the suicide questions directly and out loud. Asking does not plant the idea, and the adolescent who is thinking about it is usually waiting to be asked by somebody who will not flinch.
keyPoints: Milestone anchors: social smile 2 months, sits alone 9 months, walks 12 to 15 months, two-word phrases by 24 months.
Referral deadlines: no smile by 3 months, not sitting by 9 months, not walking by 18 months, no words by 18 months, no phrases by 24 months.
Loss of an acquired skill at any age is always abnormal, and hand preference before 12 to 18 months suggests hemiparesis.
Jaundice in the first 24 hours of life is always pathologic, as is a direct bilirubin above 1 mg/dL.
Adolescents get part of the visit alone, a HEEADSSS interview, and a stated confidentiality rule with its limits.

checks.q: A 26-month-old uses about 30 single words but no two-word phrases. What is the correct interpretation?
choices: Normal; two-word phrases appear at 3 years
A missed milestone, since two-word phrases are expected by 24 months, warranting hearing testing and developmental referral
Normal if the family is bilingual, in which case no evaluation is needed
Abnormal only if he also is not walking
checks.why: Two-word phrases are expected by 24 months, so this is a real language delay. Bilingual exposure may change the mix of words across languages but does not delay phrase combination, and language milestones are assessed independently of motor ones.

checks.q: A 3-day-old is brought in yellow. Which finding makes this pathologic rather than physiologic jaundice?
choices: Jaundice noticed on day 3
Total bilirubin rising over 48 hours
A direct (conjugated) bilirubin of 2.4 mg/dL
The infant is exclusively breastfed
checks.why: Conjugated bilirubin above 1 mg/dL is never physiologic and raises biliary atresia and other obstructive or hepatic causes. Day 3 onset, a rising total, and breastfeeding are all compatible with physiologic or breastfeeding jaundice.

checks.q: Before interviewing a 16-year-old alone, what should you say about confidentiality?
choices: Nothing; confidentiality is assumed
That everything said will be shared with the parent
That what is said stays private unless there is risk of harm to the patient or someone else, or abuse
That confidentiality applies only to sexual history
checks.why: Stating the rule and its limits up front is what makes the answers usable. Promising absolute secrecy is a promise you cannot keep, and saying nothing leaves the adolescent guessing, which usually produces a sanitized history.

lessons.title: Sizing up a child: the numbers and the triangle
lessons.body:
## Normal changes every year

A heart rate of `150` is a crisis in an adult and unremarkable in a two-month-old. A respiratory rate of `18` is normal in a teenager and a preterminal finding in an infant. You cannot assess a child without knowing which normal applies.

| Age | Heart rate | Respiratory rate | Hypotension below |
|---|---|---|---|
| Newborn to 3 mo | `100 to 160` | `30 to 60` | SBP `60` |
| 3 to 12 mo | `100 to 150` | `24 to 40` | SBP `70` |
| 1 to 3 y | `90 to 150` | `22 to 37` | SBP `70 + (2 x age)` |
| 3 to 6 y | `80 to 140` | `20 to 28` | SBP `70 + (2 x age)` |
| 6 to 12 y | `70 to 120` | `18 to 25` | SBP `70 + (2 x age)` to age 10, then `90` |
| Over 12 y | `60 to 100` | `12 to 20` | SBP `90` |

That hypotension row is the one to memorize. Hypotension in a child is a **late** finding; children hold their blood pressure by increasing heart rate and squeezing down peripheral vessels until roughly `30 to 40 percent` of blood volume is gone, and then they fall off a cliff.

## Weight is the dose

Almost every pediatric drug and fluid is `mg/kg` or `mL/kg`, so the weight is not an administrative detail, it is the prescription. Weigh in kilograms only; a pound entered as a kilogram is a greater-than-twofold overdose.

When you cannot weigh the child, estimate: for ages `1 to 10 years`, weight in kg is roughly `(age x 2) + 8`. Better, use a **length-based color-coded resuscitation tape** (the Broselow tape), which converts measured length into a weight zone and gives pre-calculated doses, tube sizes, and equipment. It is less accurate in obese children, where it tends to underestimate.

Two dosing rules that prevent harm: a weight-based dose never exceeds the adult maximum dose, and you calculate from actual measured weight rather than parental report whenever the child is stable enough to weigh.

> **Trap:** The most common pediatric medication errors are decimal-point and unit errors, not drug-choice errors. Write `0.5 mg`, never `.5 mg`, and never `5.0 mg` when you mean `5 mg`.

## The pediatric assessment triangle

Before you touch the child, you look. The pediatric assessment triangle is a structured across-the-room impression with three sides, and it takes under `30 seconds`.

**Appearance** is the most important side, because it reflects brain perfusion and oxygenation. The mnemonic is TICLS: Tone, Interactiveness, Consolability, Look or gaze, Speech or cry. A child with normal appearance is rarely critically ill at that moment.

**Work of breathing** is abnormal airway sounds (stridor, grunting, wheezing), abnormal positioning (tripod, sniffing), retractions, nasal flaring, and head bobbing.

**Circulation to skin** is pallor, mottling, and cyanosis.

The combination names the problem:

| Appearance | Breathing | Circulation | Impression |
|---|---|---|---|
| Normal | Normal | Normal | Stable |
| Normal | Abnormal | Normal | Respiratory distress |
| Abnormal | Abnormal | Normal | Respiratory failure |
| Abnormal | Normal | Abnormal | Shock |
| Abnormal | Normal | Normal | Brain or metabolic problem |
| Abnormal | Abnormal | Abnormal | Cardiopulmonary failure |

> **Key:** Grunting is the sound of a child trying to generate their own positive end-expiratory pressure. In an infant it is a sign of impending respiratory failure, not a cold.

## The quiet child

A screaming, thrashing, inconsolable child is frightening and usually well perfused. The child who has stopped fighting the exam, who does not track your face, who lets you do anything, is the emergency. Loss of interactiveness and loss of consolability precede arrest.

## Vaccines at recognition level

You need enough to spot a gap: hepatitis B at birth; DTaP, IPV, Hib, PCV, and rotavirus at `2, 4, and 6 months`; influenza annually from `6 months`; MMR, varicella, and hepatitis A at `12 to 15 months`; DTaP, IPV, MMR, and varicella boosters at `4 to 6 years`; Tdap, HPV, and MenACWY at `11 to 12 years`, with a MenACWY booster at `16`. An unimmunized febrile child changes your differential, because measles, Hib epiglottitis, and pertussis come back onto the list.
keyPoints: Pediatric hypotension thresholds: under 60 in a newborn, under 70 in an infant, under 70 + (2 x age) from 1 to 10 years, under 90 after 10.
Hypotension is late; children compensate with tachycardia until roughly 30 to 40 percent volume loss.
Estimate weight for ages 1 to 10 as (age x 2) + 8 kg, or use a length-based color-coded tape; weigh in kilograms only.
The pediatric assessment triangle is appearance (TICLS), work of breathing, and circulation to skin, done from the doorway.
Grunting and loss of consolability are late, ominous signs; the quiet child is sicker than the screaming one.

checks.q: A 4-year-old with gastroenteritis has a heart rate of 150, capillary refill of 4 seconds, and a blood pressure of 88/50. How do you characterize this?
choices: Normal for age; no intervention needed
Compensated shock, because the blood pressure is still above the 70 + (2 x age) threshold of 78 while perfusion is clearly impaired
Decompensated shock, because the systolic pressure is under 90
Isolated fever response
checks.why: For a 4-year-old, hypotension is a systolic under 78. At 88 he is still compensating, but tachycardia and a 4-second refill mean perfusion is already failing. Using the adult threshold of 90 would mislabel him and delay fluids.

checks.q: Using the age-based estimate, what is the approximate weight of a 6-year-old?
choices: 14 kg
20 kg
26 kg
32 kg
checks.why: (age x 2) + 8 gives (6 x 2) + 8 = 20 kg. This estimate is for ages 1 to 10 and is a fallback; a measured weight or a length-based tape is preferred whenever the child can be measured.

checks.q: A 10-month-old is limp, does not track your face, and has normal breath sounds and warm pink skin. Which pediatric assessment triangle pattern is this, and what does it suggest?
choices: Respiratory distress
Shock
Abnormal appearance with normal breathing and circulation, suggesting a primary brain or metabolic problem such as hypoglycemia, intoxication, or a postictal state
Stable, since two of three sides are normal
checks.why: Appearance alone is abnormal, which points at the central nervous system or metabolism rather than the lungs or the circulation. Calling it stable because two sides look fine ignores the side that reflects brain perfusion, and a glucose check is the immediate next step.

lessons.title: Fever by age and the serious infection workup
lessons.body:
## Why age drives everything

A fever in a 20-day-old and a fever in a 20-month-old are different diseases with different workups, because the immune system and the vaccine coverage are different. Newborns cannot localize infection, cannot mount a reliable fever, and carry organisms acquired at delivery: group B Streptococcus, Escherichia coli, Listeria, and herpes simplex virus.

Fever means a **rectal temperature of `38.0 C` (`100.4 F`) or higher**. Rectal is the standard under 3 years. Axillary, temporal, and tympanic readings are screening tools, not decision tools, in an infant.

## The four tiers

| Age | Workup | Disposition |
|---|---|---|
| `0 to 21 days` | Full evaluation: CBC, blood culture, catheterized urinalysis and culture, lumbar puncture with CSF culture; consider HSV testing | Empiric antibiotics and admit, every time |
| `22 to 28 days` (AAP 2021 subgroup) | Blood culture, urine, and inflammatory markers; LP strongly considered | Admit, empiric antibiotics |
| `29 to 60 days` | Blood culture, urine, inflammatory markers; LP if any marker is abnormal or the infant looks ill | If markers and urine are negative and the infant is well, may avoid LP and observe or discharge with next-day follow-up |
| `61 to 90 days` | Urinalysis and culture, blood culture; markers as indicated | Well-appearing with negative urine is usually managed outpatient |
| Over `90 days`, immunized | Look for a source; urinalysis in the right patients | Source-directed |

The inflammatory markers the 2021 AAP guideline uses are procalcitonin above `0.5 ng/mL`, C-reactive protein above `20 mg/L`, an absolute neutrophil count above roughly `4,000 to 5,200/microliter`, or a temperature above `38.5 C`.

> **Key:** Under 28 days, there is no well-appearing exception. A febrile neonate who looks perfect gets the full workup and admission, because the physical exam does not distinguish bacteremia from a virus at that age.

## Urinary tract infection, the commonest serious bacterial infection

In febrile infants without a source, urinary tract infection is the most likely serious bacterial infection, with a prevalence around `5 to 8 percent` and higher in uncircumcised boys and in girls. The specimen must be obtained by **catheterization** (or suprapubic aspiration) in a child who is not toilet trained. A bag specimen has a contamination rate high enough that a positive culture is uninterpretable; a negative bag urinalysis can be used to rule out, but a positive one must be recollected.

The AAP threshold is pyuria plus at least `50,000 CFU/mL` of a single uropathogen from a catheterized specimen.

## Meningitis in a small child

Forget neck stiffness. Kernig and Brudzinski signs are unreliable under `12 to 18 months`. What you see instead is a **bulging fontanelle**, paradoxical irritability (the infant cries more when held and rocked, because movement hurts), poor feeding, temperature instability that may be hypothermia rather than fever, and a high-pitched cry.

## Febrile seizures

Between `6 months and 5 years`, with peak incidence at `12 to 18 months`, a seizure with fever and no central nervous system infection, no metabolic cause, and no prior afebrile seizure is a febrile seizure.

**Simple** means generalized, under `15 minutes`, and only once in 24 hours. **Complex** means focal, longer than 15 minutes, or recurrent within 24 hours.

A simple febrile seizure in a well-appearing, fully immunized child over 12 months needs no routine lumbar puncture, no neuroimaging, and no EEG. Recurrence risk is about `30 to 35 percent`; the risk of later epilepsy after a simple febrile seizure is about `1 to 2 percent`, barely above the population baseline. Parents almost always believe their child is dying, and the counseling matters as much as the workup.

## Two neonatal near-misses

**Hypoglycemia** is a cause of every vague neonatal symptom: jitteriness, poor feeding, lethargy, hypothermia, seizure. Check a glucose on every sick infant. Treat symptomatic values under about `45 mg/dL` in a neonate with `D10W 2 to 5 mL/kg` IV.

A **BRUE**, a brief resolved unexplained event, is an episode in an infant under 1 year lasting under a minute, now fully resolved, with color change, absent or irregular breathing, a marked change in tone, or altered responsiveness, and no explanation after history and exam. Lower-risk criteria include age over `60 days`, a first event, duration under `1 minute`, and no CPR by a trained provider. Higher-risk infants get evaluation and observation; the label itself replaced the old term ALTE precisely because it is a description, not a diagnosis.
keyPoints: Fever in an infant is a rectal temperature of 38.0 C (100.4 F) or higher; rectal is the standard under 3 years.
Under 28 days: full workup including lumbar puncture, empiric antibiotics, and admission regardless of appearance.
29 to 60 days: risk-stratify with urinalysis and inflammatory markers (procalcitonin over 0.5 ng/mL, CRP over 20 mg/L, ANC over about 4,000 to 5,200).
Urinary tract infection is the most common serious bacterial infection in febrile infants; the specimen must be catheterized, never a bag.
Simple febrile seizure (generalized, under 15 minutes, once in 24 hours, ages 6 months to 5 years) needs no LP, imaging, or EEG in a well child.

checks.q: A 19-day-old with a rectal temperature of 38.4 C is feeding well, smiling, and has a completely normal exam. What is the correct plan?
choices: Reassurance and next-day follow-up, since he looks well
Urinalysis only; if negative, discharge
Blood and urine cultures, lumbar puncture, empiric antibiotics, and admission
Oral antibiotics and recheck in 24 hours
checks.why: Under 28 days there is no well-appearing exception, because the neonatal exam cannot exclude bacteremia, meningitis, or HSV. Partial workups and outpatient management at this age are how missed neonatal meningitis happens.

checks.q: A febrile 8-month-old girl needs a urine specimen for culture. Which method is acceptable?
choices: A bag specimen, since it is noninvasive
A catheterized specimen
A clean-catch after cleaning the perineum
A diaper squeeze specimen
checks.why: Bag and diaper specimens have contamination rates that make a positive culture uninterpretable, and a clean catch is not feasible before toilet training. Catheterization or suprapubic aspiration is required for a culture that will drive antibiotic decisions.

checks.q: An 18-month-old had a 3-minute generalized seizure during a febrile illness, is now back to baseline, is fully immunized, and has a normal exam. What is indicated?
choices: Lumbar puncture and head CT
EEG before discharge
Evaluation for the source of fever, parental counseling, and discharge without LP, imaging, or EEG
Admission for antiepileptic loading
checks.why: This meets simple febrile seizure criteria in a well, immunized child over 12 months, so routine LP, neuroimaging, and EEG add risk and cost without changing management. Antiepileptics are not indicated for simple febrile seizures.

lessons.title: Pediatric breathing emergencies
lessons.body:
## Small airways, big consequences

Airway resistance rises with the fourth power of the radius, so `1 mm` of edema in an infant trachea does far more than `1 mm` in an adult. This is why children get into respiratory trouble quickly and why the location of the narrowing tells you the disease: noise on inspiration is above the vocal cords, noise on expiration is below them.

## Bronchiolitis

Under `2 years`, peak at `2 to 6 months`, usually respiratory syncytial virus, usually winter. Small-airway inflammation and mucus plugging produce wheezing, crackles, tachypnea, retractions, and a poor feed.

The treatment is unglamorous and evidence-based: **nasal suctioning**, hydration, and oxygen for hypoxia. Routine bronchodilators, corticosteroids, antibiotics, and chest radiographs are not recommended. Infants are obligate nasal breathers, which is why suctioning the nose is the single most useful thing done for them.

The complication to anticipate is **apnea**, most likely in infants under `2 months` and in those born prematurely. Day 3 to 5 of illness is typically the worst.

## Croup

Laryngotracheobronchitis, usually parainfluenza, `6 months to 3 years`, classically at night. Subglottic edema gives a barky seal-like cough, hoarse voice, and inspiratory stridor.

The Westley croup score grades level of consciousness, cyanosis, stridor, air entry, and retractions from `0 to 17`: mild is `2 or less`, moderate `3 to 5`, severe `6 to 11`, impending failure `12 or more`.

**Dexamethasone `0.6 mg/kg`** as a single oral, IM, or IV dose is given for every severity including mild, because it shortens symptoms and reduces return visits. Nebulized epinephrine is added for stridor at rest; because its effect wears off before the disease does, observe for `2 to 4 hours` afterward for rebound before discharging.

> **Trap:** Stridor that is present only when the child cries is mild. Stridor at rest is moderate or worse. That distinction, not the drama of the cough, drives disposition.

## Asthma

Severity is judged by mental status, work of breathing, air movement, speech, and oxygen saturation, formalized in scores such as the pediatric asthma score. A wheeze that disappears without the child improving is not good news: a **silent chest** means air movement has stopped.

First-hour treatment is albuterol (`2.5 mg` nebulized under 20 kg, `5 mg` at or above 20 kg, or `4 to 8` metered-dose inhaler puffs with a spacer), ipratropium `0.5 mg` added for moderate to severe presentations for up to three doses, and a systemic corticosteroid **within the first hour**: prednisone or prednisolone `1 to 2 mg/kg` (max `60 mg`) or dexamethasone `0.6 mg/kg` (max `16 mg`). Magnesium sulfate `25 to 50 mg/kg` IV (max `2 g`) is added for severe exacerbations.

## Pneumonia

**Tachypnea is the most sensitive sign**, more than crackles and more than the chest radiograph. The World Health Organization age cutoffs are a respiratory rate over `60` under 2 months, over `50` from 2 to 12 months, and over `40` from 1 to 5 years. First-line outpatient therapy for typical community-acquired pneumonia is high-dose amoxicillin, roughly `90 mg/kg/day` divided.

## Pertussis

Three stages: catarrhal (looks like a cold, most contagious), paroxysmal (coughing fits, inspiratory whoop, post-tussive vomiting), convalescent (weeks of residual cough). Marked lymphocytosis on the CBC is a clue.

Infants under `1 year` carry the highest mortality, and they often do not whoop. They present with **apnea, cyanosis, and feeding-associated coughing spells**. Treatment is azithromycin, which reduces transmission more than it shortens illness. Tdap given to the mother at `27 to 36 weeks` of every pregnancy is the main protection for a newborn.

## Foreign body aspiration

Toddlers, sudden onset while eating or playing, often a witnessed choking episode. Findings are unilateral: focal wheeze, decreased breath sounds on one side, a persistent cough after an abrupt start. The right mainstem is the usual destination. Most aspirated objects are radiolucent, so a normal chest film does not exclude it; inspiratory and expiratory films may show air trapping on the affected side. Rigid bronchoscopy is both diagnostic and therapeutic.

> **On shift:** A first-ever wheeze in a toddler with no viral symptoms and no atopy history is a foreign body until somebody proves otherwise. Asthma rarely starts with one loud wheeze on one side, in one afternoon.
keyPoints: Bronchiolitis: under 2 years, RSV; nasal suctioning, hydration, oxygen. No routine bronchodilators, steroids, antibiotics, or x-ray. Watch for apnea under 2 months.
Croup: dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg for every severity; nebulized epinephrine for stridor at rest, then observe 2 to 4 hours for rebound.
Asthma: albuterol plus ipratropium 0.5 mg for moderate-severe, systemic steroid within the first hour, magnesium 25 to 50 mg/kg for severe. A silent chest is ominous.
Tachypnea is the most sensitive sign of pediatric pneumonia; amoxicillin about 90 mg/kg/day is first line.
Infants with pertussis present with apnea and cyanosis, not a whoop; a sudden unilateral wheeze in a toddler is a foreign body until excluded.

checks.q: A 5-month-old with 3 days of cough has diffuse wheezes, crackles, a respiratory rate of 58, and a saturation of 94 percent on room air. What is the most useful intervention?
choices: Nebulized albuterol
Oral corticosteroid
Nasal suctioning and support of feeding and hydration
Amoxicillin and a chest radiograph
checks.why: This is bronchiolitis, where suctioning an obligate nasal breather and maintaining hydration are the interventions that help. Bronchodilators and steroids have not shown benefit in bronchiolitis, and antibiotics and imaging add cost and risk without changing management.

checks.q: A 2-year-old has a barky cough and inspiratory stridor at rest with mild retractions. Which combination is correct?
choices: Dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg only, then discharge immediately
Dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg plus nebulized epinephrine, with 2 to 4 hours of observation for rebound
Nebulized epinephrine alone, then discharge
Antibiotics and a lateral neck radiograph
checks.why: Stridor at rest is moderate croup, which earns epinephrine in addition to the steroid every patient gets. Because epinephrine wears off before the edema does, discharging immediately risks return with worse stridor. Croup is viral, so antibiotics do nothing.

checks.q: An 18-month-old develops sudden coughing at lunch and now has a focal wheeze and decreased breath sounds on the right. The chest radiograph is read as normal. What is the next step?
choices: Diagnose new-onset asthma and start albuterol
Reassure; a normal radiograph excludes foreign body
Treat for pneumonia with amoxicillin
Arrange bronchoscopy, because most aspirated foreign bodies are radiolucent
checks.why: A normal film does not exclude aspiration, since food and plastic are radiolucent. The abrupt onset with unilateral findings is the classic picture, and rigid bronchoscopy is both the diagnostic and the therapeutic step. Asthma and pneumonia do not begin this way.

lessons.title: Dehydration and the pediatric abdomen
lessons.body:
## Why children dry out faster

A child has a higher body-surface-area-to-mass ratio, a higher metabolic rate, and no ability to get their own drink. Total body water is a larger fraction of weight, and turnover is faster, so a percentage loss that an adult shrugs off is a resuscitation in a toddler.

Percent dehydration is estimated clinically, and the numbers below are the ones you will be asked for.

| Severity | Deficit | Findings |
|---|---|---|
| Mild | about `3 to 5 percent` | Normal vitals, slightly dry lips, normal capillary refill and urine output |
| Moderate | about `6 to 9 percent` | Dry mucous membranes, decreased tears, tachycardia, capillary refill `2 to 3 s`, sunken eyes or fontanelle, decreased urine, decreased turgor |
| Severe | `10 percent or more` | Lethargy, capillary refill over `3 s`, marked tachycardia, cool mottled skin, anuria, tenting; hypotension is a late finding |

The three best individual signs are prolonged capillary refill, abnormal skin turgor, and abnormal respiratory pattern.

## Oral rehydration is the default

For mild and moderate dehydration without shock, oral rehydration therapy works as well as IV fluid and avoids a needle. Give an oral rehydration solution: about `50 mL/kg` over 4 hours for mild and `100 mL/kg` over 4 hours for moderate, plus replacement of ongoing losses, roughly `10 mL/kg` per stool.

The technique is what makes it succeed: `5 mL` by syringe every `1 to 2 minutes`, not a cup handed to a vomiting child. A single dose of **ondansetron `0.15 mg/kg`** (commonly `2 mg` for 8 to 15 kg, `4 mg` for 15 to 30 kg, `8 mg` over 30 kg) substantially raises the success rate of oral rehydration and reduces IV starts and admissions.

Severe dehydration or shock is IV: isotonic crystalloid `20 mL/kg` as a bolus, reassessed after each bolus. Plain water, juice, and soda are wrong answers; they worsen hyponatremia and the sugar load worsens the diarrhea.

> **Key:** In pediatric gastroenteritis, an antiemetic and a syringe beat an intravenous line most of the time. Reserve IV fluids for shock, failed oral trials, and altered mental status.

## Four surgical abdomens by age

**Malrotation with midgut volvulus.** Neonate, usually in the first month. **Bilious vomiting in a neonate is volvulus until proven otherwise.** Green vomit is a surgical emergency, not reflux. Upper gastrointestinal series is the diagnostic study; the bowel can infarct within hours.

**Pyloric stenosis.** `3 to 6 weeks` old, more often firstborn males. Progressive **nonbilious** projectile vomiting in an infant who is hungry again immediately after vomiting. The classic laboratory finding is a **hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis**. Ultrasound shows a thickened, elongated pylorus. Correct the electrolytes first; the pyloromyotomy is urgent but not emergent, and operating on an alkalotic infant risks postoperative apnea.

**Intussusception.** `6 months to 3 years`, peak around `5 to 9 months`, usually ileocolic. Intermittent severe colicky pain in which the child draws up the legs, alternating with intervals of being limp and lethargic. The currant-jelly stool is late and appears in under a quarter of cases; do not wait for it. Ultrasound shows a target or donut sign and is the test of choice; air or contrast enema is both diagnostic and therapeutic.

**Appendicitis.** Harder in children and much more likely to perforate, approaching `80 percent or more` under age 3, because the history is unreliable and the omentum is underdeveloped. Ultrasound is first-line imaging in children to avoid CT radiation, with CT or MRI when ultrasound is equivocal. Scoring tools such as the pediatric appendicitis score help stratify but do not replace reassessment.

> **Trap:** Lethargy without obvious pain can be the only presentation of intussusception. An infant who is intermittently limp and inconsolable with vomiting deserves an ultrasound even when the abdomen is soft between episodes.

## Gastroenteritis and when it is not

Most pediatric vomiting and diarrhea is viral, now most often norovirus. Bloody diarrhea suggests a bacterial cause, and in suspected Shiga-toxin-producing Escherichia coli, **antibiotics and antimotility agents are avoided** because they increase the risk of hemolytic uremic syndrome. Vomiting without diarrhea should make you look harder: that pattern belongs to obstruction, raised intracranial pressure, diabetic ketoacidosis, and urinary tract infection as often as to gastroenteritis.
keyPoints: Dehydration: mild 3 to 5 percent, moderate 6 to 9 percent, severe 10 percent or more; capillary refill, turgor, and respiratory pattern are the best signs.
Oral rehydration 50 mL/kg (mild) or 100 mL/kg (moderate) over 4 hours, given as 5 mL by syringe every 1 to 2 minutes.
Ondansetron 0.15 mg/kg as a single dose raises oral rehydration success and reduces IV starts; severe dehydration gets 20 mL/kg isotonic boluses.
Bilious vomiting in a neonate is midgut volvulus until excluded; nonbilious projectile vomiting at 3 to 6 weeks with hypochloremic hypokalemic alkalosis is pyloric stenosis.
Intussusception can present as intermittent lethargy alone; ultrasound is the test of choice and enema is therapeutic.

checks.q: A 2-year-old with gastroenteritis has dry mucous membranes, capillary refill of 3 seconds, a heart rate of 150, and is alert. He vomited twice in the waiting room. What is the best initial management?
choices: Immediate IV line and a 20 mL/kg bolus
Ondansetron, then oral rehydration solution about 100 mL/kg over 4 hours given 5 mL at a time by syringe
Apple juice by cup, as much as tolerated
Nothing by mouth for 6 hours, then reassess
checks.why: This is moderate dehydration without shock, where oral rehydration matches IV fluid in outcome and an antiemetic makes it work. Juice worsens diarrhea and hyponatremia, and withholding fluid in a dehydrated child makes the deficit worse.

checks.q: A 5-week-old boy has 10 days of worsening nonbilious projectile vomiting and is ravenous after each episode. What laboratory pattern do you expect?
choices: Hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis
Hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis
Anion-gap metabolic acidosis with ketones
Normal electrolytes
checks.why: Loss of gastric hydrochloric acid produces hypochloremic hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis, the classic pattern of pyloric stenosis. Those electrolytes must be corrected before pyloromyotomy, since alkalosis predisposes to postoperative apnea.

checks.q: An 8-month-old has episodes of drawing up his legs and screaming, with intervals of limpness and lethargy between them. His abdomen is soft. What is the next step?
choices: Reassure and treat as colic
Wait for currant-jelly stool before imaging
Abdominal ultrasound looking for a target sign
Plain abdominal radiograph, which reliably excludes intussusception
checks.why: Intermittent colicky pain alternating with lethargy in this age range is intussusception until excluded, and ultrasound is the test of choice. Currant-jelly stool is late and uncommon, and plain films cannot exclude the diagnosis.

lessons.title: Rashes, red flags, and the injured child
lessons.body:
## Press on it

The first question about any pediatric rash is whether it blanches. Press a glass or your thumb against it. A rash that whitens under pressure is inside vessels; a rash that stays is blood outside vessels, meaning petechiae or purpura.

**Fever plus a non-blanching rash is meningococcemia until excluded.** That is a blood culture, antibiotics without waiting, droplet precautions, and prophylaxis for close contacts. Petechiae confined to above the nipple line after forceful vomiting or coughing are usually mechanical and benign, but that exception requires a well child.

## The classic exanthems

| Disease | Age and cause | The tell |
|---|---|---|
| Measles | Unimmunized, paramyxovirus | Prodrome of cough, coryza, conjunctivitis; Koplik spots; rash starts at the hairline day 3 to 5 and moves down. Airborne isolation immediately, vitamin A |
| Varicella | Any, VZV | Crops of lesions in **different stages** at once, intensely itchy, vesicle on a red base |
| Hand-foot-and-mouth | 10 months to 5 years, coxsackievirus | Oral ulcers plus vesicles on palms, soles, buttocks; supportive care |
| Scarlet fever | 5 to 15 years, group A strep | Sandpaper rash, strawberry tongue, circumoral pallor, Pastia lines in skin folds; penicillin or amoxicillin |
| IgA vasculitis (HSP) | 3 to 10 years | **Palpable purpura** on buttocks and legs, arthralgia, abdominal pain, hematuria. Follow blood pressure and urine; can cause ileoileal intussusception |

## Kawasaki disease

Fever for `5 days or more` plus four of five: bilateral nonexudative conjunctivitis, oral changes (cracked lips, strawberry tongue), a polymorphous rash, extremity changes (swelling, then periungual peeling), and cervical lymphadenopathy over `1.5 cm`, usually one-sided.

Untreated it causes coronary aneurysms in roughly `25 percent` of cases, falling to about `4 percent` with IVIG `2 g/kg` plus aspirin within the first `10 days`. Prolonged unexplained fever under age 5 should always raise it.

> **Key:** Two pediatric fevers demand a decision the same day: fever with non-blanching purpura (meningococcemia) and fever for five days with red eyes and lips (Kawasaki). Both are made worse by waiting for a pattern to declare itself.

## Ears, throat, and eyes

Acute **otitis media** requires a bulging, immobile tympanic membrane, not simply a red one; a crying child has red drums. Treat with high-dose amoxicillin.

**Strep pharyngitis** is rare under age 3 and needs a test before antibiotics. **Peritonsillar abscess** is an adolescent problem: trismus, a hot-potato voice, a deviated uvula. **Retropharyngeal abscess** is a younger child who will not extend the neck.

**Preseptal (periorbital) cellulitis** is eyelid swelling with a normal globe. **Orbital (postseptal) cellulitis** adds pain with eye movement, proptosis, restricted motion, or reduced acuity, which means CT of the orbits, IV antibiotics, and ophthalmology.

## Head injury and PECARN

The PECARN rule identifies children with blunt head trauma, GCS `14 to 15`, who can safely skip a CT. Immediate CT is indicated for GCS `14 or less`, altered mental status, a palpable skull fracture under age 2, or signs of basilar skull fracture at age 2 or older.

Intermediate predictors mean CT versus observation, shared with the family: under 2 years, an occipital, parietal, or temporal scalp hematoma, loss of consciousness for `5 seconds or more`, severe mechanism, or acting abnormally per the parent. At 2 years or older, any loss of consciousness, vomiting, severe headache, or severe mechanism.

With none of the predictors, the risk of clinically important traumatic brain injury is under `0.05 percent` and CT is not recommended.

## The child you must report

The most powerful abuse screen is developmental: **a child who is not cruising rarely bruises**. Any bruise in an infant under `4 months` is a red flag, as is the TEN-4 pattern, bruising of the torso, ears, or neck in a child `4 years or younger`.

Other findings: an injury that does not match the mechanism, a changing history, delayed presentation, patterned or immersion burns, posterior rib fractures, metaphyseal corner lesions, retinal hemorrhages, and fractures of different ages. Skeletal survey is standard under `2 years`.

**New Jersey is a universal mandatory reporting state.** Any person with reasonable cause to believe a child has been abused or neglected must report immediately to the State Central Registry at `1-877-NJ-ABUSE` (`1-877-652-2873`), staffed 24 hours. You do not need proof, you do not need your supervisor's agreement, and good-faith reporting carries immunity from liability. Failing to report is itself an offense.
keyPoints: Blanching versus non-blanching is the first question; fever plus non-blanching purpura is meningococcemia until excluded.
Kawasaki: fever 5 days or more plus 4 of 5 criteria; IVIG 2 g/kg with aspirin within 10 days cuts coronary aneurysm risk from about 25 percent to about 4 percent.
Orbital cellulitis is distinguished from preseptal by pain with eye movement, proptosis, restricted motion, or reduced acuity, and needs CT and IV antibiotics.
PECARN: GCS 14 or less, altered mental status, palpable skull fracture under 2, or basilar signs at 2 or older means CT; no predictors means risk under 0.05 percent.
In New Jersey, any person with reasonable cause must report suspected child abuse to 1-877-NJ-ABUSE immediately; good-faith reports are immune from liability.

checks.q: A 3-year-old has a fever of 39.2 C and scattered purple spots on the legs that do not blanch under glass. What is the immediate action?
choices: Reassure; petechiae after fever are usually viral
Blood cultures and empiric antibiotics without delay, with droplet precautions
Send home with 24-hour follow-up
Obtain a platelet count first and decide afterward
checks.why: Fever with non-blanching purpura is meningococcemia until excluded, and mortality rises with every hour of delay. Waiting on a platelet count or a follow-up visit trades a treatable hour for a disease that can kill within one.

checks.q: A 4-year-old has eyelid swelling, pain when she looks to the side, and mild proptosis. What does this indicate?
choices: Preseptal cellulitis; oral antibiotics and follow-up
Allergic edema; antihistamines
Orbital (postseptal) cellulitis; CT of the orbits, IV antibiotics, ophthalmology
Conjunctivitis; topical antibiotics
checks.why: Pain with eye movement and proptosis mean involvement behind the orbital septum, which risks vision loss, cavernous sinus thrombosis, and abscess. Preseptal disease has a normal globe, and allergy and conjunctivitis do not cause proptosis.

checks.q: A 3-month-old has a 2 cm bruise on the left cheek. The father says the infant rolled into the crib rail. What is required of you?
choices: Document and reassure, since infants bruise easily
Report to the State Central Registry, because bruising in an infant under 4 months is a red flag and the mechanism does not match the developmental stage
Ask the mother privately and report only if she agrees
Consult your supervisor and report only if the supervisor concurs
checks.why: Bruising in a non-ambulatory infant is highly concerning, and the stated mechanism exceeds what a 3-month-old can do. New Jersey requires any person with reasonable cause to report immediately; consent from a parent or agreement from a supervisor is not a prerequisite.

lessons.title: Why old bodies present differently
lessons.body:
## Reserve, not disease

Aging is not illness. What aging removes is **reserve**: the margin between how a system performs at rest and what it can do under stress. Every classic geriatric presentation follows from that one idea. An older adult is not sicker at baseline; they simply have less room between baseline and failure, and the failure shows up in whichever organ has the least margin, which is often the brain.

## System by system

| System | What changes | What it produces |
|---|---|---|
| Cardiovascular | Arterial stiffening, diastolic dysfunction, fewer responsive beta receptors | Isolated systolic hypertension, a blunted heart-rate response to stress, dependence on preload |
| Respiratory | Stiffer chest wall, lower vital capacity, blunted hypoxic and hypercapnic drive, weaker cough | Aspiration, pneumonia without cough, late hypoxia |
| Renal | Glomerular filtration falls roughly `8 mL/min` per decade after age 40; less concentrating ability | Drug accumulation, easy dehydration, acute kidney injury |
| Neurologic | Brain atrophy stretches bridging veins; less cognitive reserve | Subdural hematoma from minor trauma, delirium from any insult |
| Immune | Immunosenescence, blunted fever response | Afebrile sepsis, normal white count with bacteremia |
| Thermoregulatory | Lower baseline temperature | Fever thresholds must be lowered |

> **Key:** A **normal serum creatinine does not mean normal kidney function** in an older adult. Creatinine is made by muscle, and muscle mass is down, so a creatinine of `1.0 mg/dL` in an 85-year-old can hide a glomerular filtration rate near `40`. Estimate GFR before dosing renally cleared drugs.

## Fever is a lower number

Up to `20 to 30 percent` of older adults with serious infection are afebrile. Because baseline temperature is lower, the accepted thresholds in this population are a single oral temperature above `37.8 C` (`100 F`), repeated oral temperatures above `37.2 C` (`99 F`), a rectal temperature above `37.5 C` (`99.5 F`), or a rise of `1.1 C` (`2 F`) over the patient's own baseline.

Hypothermia in an older adult with infection is a worse prognostic sign than fever.

## The three silent presentations

**Silent myocardial infarction.** Roughly a third of infarcts in older adults occur without chest pain. What appears instead is dyspnea, syncope, fatigue, nausea, or acute confusion. An ECG belongs in the workup of an older adult with weakness or a fall, not only one with chest pain.

**Afebrile sepsis.** The presentation may be confusion, a fall, decreased oral intake, or simply not being themselves. Tachycardia may be absent if the patient takes a beta blocker, and the white count may be normal with a left shift.

**The painless abdomen.** Abdominal musculature is weaker, so peritonitis may not produce rigidity or guarding. Perforation and mesenteric ischemia can present with vague pain, a soft abdomen, and a lactate that does not match the exam. Mesenteric ischemia classically shows pain out of proportion to the examination, in a patient with atrial fibrillation or vascular disease.

> **Trap:** In an older adult, the sentence "she just is not herself" is a chief complaint, not a lack of one. Acute change in mental or functional status is a presenting symptom of infection, infarction, bleeding, and drug toxicity.

## Geriatric trauma triage

Age `65 and older` independently increases mortality at any given injury severity, so triage thresholds move. Field triage criteria treat a systolic pressure under `110 mmHg` in patients over 65 as hypotension, rather than the usual `90`, because a stiff hypertensive vasculature makes `110` a profound drop for someone whose baseline is `160`.

Mechanism misleads too. A **ground-level fall** is the dominant mechanism of serious injury in this age group, and it produces cervical spine fractures, subdural hematomas, and hip fractures. Rib fractures are not minor: each additional fractured rib in an older adult raises mortality on the order of `19 percent` and pneumonia risk around `27 percent`.

## The anticoagulant question

Any head strike in a patient on an anticoagulant or antiplatelet agent gets a head CT, even with a GCS of `15`, no loss of consciousness, and a normal neurologic exam. The Canadian CT Head Rule explicitly excludes anticoagulated patients, so it cannot be used to avoid imaging here.

If bleeding is found, reversal is agent-specific: warfarin takes four-factor prothrombin complex concentrate plus vitamin K `10 mg` IV; dabigatran takes idarucizumab `5 g`; apixaban and rivaroxaban take andexanet alfa or four-factor PCC. Delayed intracranial hemorrhage after an initially negative CT is uncommon but real, and observation practice varies by institution.
keyPoints: Aging removes reserve, not function; the failure appears in the organ with the least margin, often the brain.
A normal creatinine can hide a low GFR because muscle mass is reduced; estimate GFR before dosing.
Fever thresholds are lower in older adults: oral above 37.8 C once, above 37.2 C repeatedly, or 1.1 C above baseline; 20 to 30 percent of serious infections are afebrile.
About a third of myocardial infarctions in older adults are painless, presenting as dyspnea, syncope, weakness, or confusion.
Age 65 and older shifts trauma triage: systolic under 110 counts as hypotension, and any head strike on an anticoagulant gets a CT.

checks.q: An 84-year-old woman on metoprolol presents with 2 days of confusion and decreased intake. Temperature 37.4 C, heart rate 84, white count 9,800. Which conclusion is best supported?
choices: Infection is effectively excluded by the normal vitals and white count
This is likely dementia progression
Serious infection remains fully possible, since older adults are often afebrile, a beta blocker blunts tachycardia, and the white count can be normal
The confusion is psychiatric
checks.why: Immunosenescence, a lower baseline temperature, and beta blockade each remove one of the signs you would normally rely on. Dementia does not progress over two days, and acute change is the presenting symptom of infection in this population.

checks.q: A 79-year-old man on apixaban trips over a curb, strikes his forehead, has no loss of consciousness, and has a GCS of 15 with a normal neurologic exam. What is indicated?
choices: Discharge with head injury precautions
Apply the Canadian CT Head Rule; no imaging if he scores low
Non-contrast head CT
Skull radiographs
checks.why: Anticoagulation plus any head strike is an indication for CT regardless of a reassuring exam. The Canadian rule was derived in a population that excluded anticoagulated patients, and skull films do not detect intracranial blood.

checks.q: An 82-year-old with a baseline blood pressure of 165/85 arrives after a fall with a blood pressure of 108/62 and a heart rate of 92. How should this be read?
choices: Normal; systolic pressure is above 90
Relative hypotension, since a systolic under 110 in patients over 65 meets trauma triage criteria and represents a large drop from baseline
Expected postural change requiring no action
Evidence against significant injury, because the heart rate is under 100
checks.why: Trauma triage uses 110 rather than 90 after age 65 precisely because a stiff, chronically hypertensive circulation makes 108 a profound fall from a baseline of 165. A heart rate of 92 may already be relative tachycardia if the patient takes a beta blocker.

lessons.title: The geriatric syndromes
lessons.body:
## What a syndrome means here

A geriatric syndrome is a single visible problem, such as a fall or confusion, produced by many small failures across several systems at once. That is why the right question is never "what caused the fall" but "what were the six things that had to go wrong together."

## Falls

About `1 in 4` adults aged 65 and over falls each year, and falls are the leading cause of injury death in that group. The clinical trap is treating the injury and discharging without ever answering why the person fell.

The first branch point: **was this mechanical or was this syncope?** A patient who tripped and remembers everything is different from one who woke up on the floor. Anyone who cannot account for the event gets an ECG, a glucose, and a look for arrhythmia, bleeding, and infection.

The rest of the workup is a list of contributors: orthostatic vital signs, medications (antihypertensives, sedatives, anticholinergics, diuretics), vision, footwear, gait and balance (a Timed Up and Go over `12 seconds` is abnormal), peripheral neuropathy, alcohol, and environmental hazards. Discharge without a modified plan is how the second fall happens.

**Hip fracture** is the outcome to fear: roughly `20 to 30 percent` one-year mortality, best outcomes with surgery within `24 to 48 hours`, classically a shortened and externally rotated leg. A regional block such as a fascia iliaca block reduces opioid use and therefore delirium. If the film is negative but the patient cannot bear weight, an occult fracture needs MRI.

## Delirium

Delirium is acute brain failure. It is present in roughly `8 to 17 percent` of older emergency department patients and is missed in the majority of cases, and missing it matters: one-year mortality after an episode is on the order of `35 to 40 percent`.

The Confusion Assessment Method requires **feature 1 and feature 2, plus either feature 3 or feature 4**:

1. Acute onset and a fluctuating course
2. Inattention
3. Disorganized thinking
4. Altered level of consciousness

**Hypoactive delirium** is the quiet, withdrawn, sleepy form. It is more common than the agitated form, far more often missed, and has the worse prognosis. The agitated patient gets attention; the quiet one gets called pleasant and confused and is sent back to the facility.

| | Delirium | Dementia | Depression |
|---|---|---|---|
| Onset | Hours to days | Months to years | Weeks to months |
| Course | Fluctuates within a day | Slowly progressive | Fairly steady |
| Attention | Impaired, the hallmark | Intact until late | Variable |
| Consciousness | Altered | Clear | Clear |
| Reversible | Usually | No | Usually |

> **Key:** Inattention is the feature that separates delirium from dementia at the bedside. Ask the months of the year backward or a digit span. A patient who cannot hold the thread of the question is delirious regardless of their baseline diagnosis.

The common causes are ordinary: infection, medications (anticholinergics, benzodiazepines, opioids), dehydration and electrolyte disturbance, hypoxia, urinary retention, constipation, uncontrolled pain, stroke, and myocardial infarction. Non-drug management comes first: glasses, hearing aids, lights on in the day, family present, mobility, sleep, and removing the catheter.

## Frailty

Frailty is measurable, not a vibe. The Fried phenotype counts five items and calls three or more frail: unintentional weight loss of about `10 pounds` in a year, self-reported exhaustion, weak grip strength, slow walking speed, and low physical activity. The Clinical Frailty Scale runs `1` (very fit) to `9` (terminally ill). Frailty predicts surgical complications, readmission, and mortality better than age does, and it is the reason two 85-year-olds get different plans.

## Incontinence, nutrition, and skin

New incontinence is a symptom, and the reversible causes are remembered as DIAPPERS: Delirium, Infection, Atrophic vaginitis, Pharmaceuticals, Psychological, Excess urine output, Restricted mobility, Stool impaction.

Malnutrition is common, under-recognized, and drives poor healing, falls, and infection. Ask who shops and who cooks.

Pressure injuries stage `1` (non-blanching erythema of intact skin) through `4` (exposed bone, tendon, or muscle), plus unstageable and deep tissue injury. They form over the sacrum and heels in hours of immobility, including on an emergency department stretcher. **Document them on arrival**; an injury not documented at presentation is presumed to have developed under your care.
keyPoints: A geriatric syndrome is one visible problem produced by several small failures at once.
After a fall, answer why: mechanical versus syncope, then orthostatics, medications, gait, vision, and an ECG for anything unwitnessed.
CAM requires acute fluctuating onset plus inattention, plus either disorganized thinking or altered consciousness; hypoactive delirium is commoner and more often missed.
Delirium fluctuates and impairs attention; dementia is slowly progressive with attention intact until late.
Hip fracture carries 20 to 30 percent one-year mortality; pressure injuries must be documented on arrival.

checks.q: An 88-year-old nursing home resident is quiet, sleepy, and answers slowly but is not agitated. Over the afternoon she is alert at times and barely rousable at others. What is the most likely diagnosis?
choices: Progression of dementia
Hypoactive delirium
Depression
Normal aging
checks.why: Acute onset with fluctuation and impaired attention is delirium, and the quiet form is the more common and more dangerous one. Dementia progresses over months without hour-to-hour fluctuation, and depression does not alter level of consciousness.

checks.q: Which bedside test best separates delirium from dementia?
choices: Long-term memory recall
Orientation to place
A test of attention, such as reciting the months backward
Naming three objects
checks.why: Inattention is the hallmark of delirium and is relatively preserved in early and moderate dementia. Orientation and memory are impaired in both, so they cannot discriminate; sustained attention can.

checks.q: A 76-year-old is treated for a wrist fracture after falling at home and is about to be discharged. What is the most important remaining step?
choices: Prescribe an opioid for pain control
Determine why he fell, including orthostatic vitals, a medication review, and an ECG if the event is unexplained
Arrange orthopedic follow-up only
Order a bone density scan before discharge
checks.why: Treating the fracture without explaining the fall leaves the mechanism in place and predicts a repeat fall, often with a worse injury. Opioids increase delirium and fall risk, and bone density testing is an outpatient issue, not the acute question.

lessons.title: Polypharmacy, Beers, and the medication-caused emergency
lessons.body:
## The most common reversible cause

Older adults take more drugs, clear them more slowly, and have less reserve to absorb an adverse effect. Polypharmacy is usually defined as `5 or more` regular medications, and adverse drug events account for a large share of geriatric emergency visits. Before you add a diagnosis, look at the list: the drug that was started three weeks ago explains a surprising number of presentations.

Two pharmacologic facts drive the risk. Renal clearance falls with age even when creatinine looks normal, so renally cleared drugs accumulate. And body composition shifts toward fat, so lipid-soluble drugs such as diazepam have a longer half-life and a larger volume of distribution, meaning a single dose lingers for days.

## Beers criteria

The American Geriatrics Society Beers criteria list potentially inappropriate medications in adults `65 and older`. They are not a ban; they are a prompt to justify. The highest-yield entries:

| Drug or class | Why it is on the list |
|---|---|
| Benzodiazepines | Falls, fractures, delirium, prolonged sedation |
| Z-drugs (zolpidem, eszopiclone) | Same harms as benzodiazepines, no better sleep |
| First-generation antihistamines (diphenhydramine, hydroxyzine) | Strongly anticholinergic; confusion, retention, constipation |
| Anticholinergics generally (oxybutynin, amitriptyline, cyclobenzaprine) | Delirium, urinary retention, falls |
| Antipsychotics for dementia-related behavior | Increased mortality; boxed warning |
| NSAIDs | GI bleeding, acute kidney injury, heart failure, hypertension |
| Sulfonylureas, especially glyburide | Prolonged, severe hypoglycemia |
| Skeletal muscle relaxants | Sedation, anticholinergic effects, weakness |
| Meperidine | Neurotoxic metabolite, seizures |
| Digoxin above `0.125 mg` daily | Toxicity with declining renal function |
| Proton pump inhibitors beyond `8 weeks` without indication | C. difficile, fractures, B12 deficiency |

> **Trap:** Diphenhydramine is available without a prescription, appears in every over-the-counter sleep and cold product, and is one of the most reliable ways to make an 80-year-old delirious. Always ask specifically about non-prescription products, which patients do not consider medications.

## The prescribing cascade

A prescribing cascade is when a side effect is treated as a new disease. A calcium channel blocker causes ankle edema, so a diuretic is added; the diuretic causes urgency, so oxybutynin is added; oxybutynin causes confusion and retention, so an antipsychotic is added. Four drugs, one original problem.

Breaking a cascade means asking of every new symptom: could a drug be doing this. **Start low, go slow**, and treat deprescribing as an intervention with its own indication.

## Dehydration and electrolytes

Thirst is blunted, concentrating ability is reduced, and mobility limits access to fluid, so older adults dehydrate quietly. Two patterns dominate.

**Hyponatremia** comes from thiazides, SSRIs, and SIADH, and presents as confusion, gait change, or seizure. Correct slowly; overly rapid correction risks osmotic demyelination.

**Acute kidney injury** frequently comes from the combination of an ACE inhibitor or ARB, a diuretic, and an NSAID, sometimes called the triple whammy, on top of a day of poor intake or vomiting.

## The urine culture problem

**Asymptomatic bacteriuria** is bacteria in the urine without urinary symptoms. Its prevalence reaches `15 percent` in community-dwelling older women and `25 to 50 percent` in nursing home residents. Guidelines are explicit: do not screen for it and do not treat it, except in pregnancy and before urologic procedures expected to cause mucosal bleeding.

This matters because confusion plus a positive urine culture is the most common false explanation in geriatric medicine. Confusion without dysuria, urgency, frequency, suprapubic or flank pain, or systemic signs of infection is a **delirium workup**, not a urinary tract infection. Treating the urine ends the search, the real cause goes unfound, and the patient also gets C. difficile risk and resistance for nothing.

> **Key:** In a delirious older adult, a positive urine culture is a finding, not an answer. Ask what else is on the list before you accept it.
keyPoints: Polypharmacy is 5 or more regular medications; adverse drug events are a leading cause of geriatric emergency visits.
Highest-risk Beers classes: benzodiazepines and Z-drugs, anticholinergics including diphenhydramine, antipsychotics in dementia, NSAIDs, and glyburide.
A prescribing cascade treats a drug side effect as a new disease; ask of every symptom whether a medication could be causing it.
The triple whammy of ACE inhibitor or ARB plus diuretic plus NSAID is a common cause of acute kidney injury.
Asymptomatic bacteriuria is common and should not be treated; confusion with a positive urine culture still requires a full delirium workup.

checks.q: An 81-year-old with mild dementia becomes acutely confused and cannot urinate. She started an over-the-counter sleep aid last week. What is the most likely cause?
choices: Progression of her dementia
Anticholinergic toxicity from diphenhydramine, the usual active ingredient in over-the-counter sleep aids
A urinary tract infection
Normal pressure hydrocephalus
checks.why: Confusion plus urinary retention beginning days after starting a nighttime antihistamine is textbook anticholinergic toxicity. Dementia does not progress over a week, and retention with acute confusion points to the drug before it points to infection.

checks.q: A nursing home resident with new confusion and no urinary symptoms has a urine culture growing 100,000 CFU/mL of E. coli. What is the correct interpretation?
choices: A urinary tract infection; treat with antibiotics and stop the workup
Likely asymptomatic bacteriuria; continue the full delirium workup rather than accepting the urine as the explanation
Contamination; repeat the culture and do nothing else
Urosepsis; start broad-spectrum antibiotics and admit
checks.why: Asymptomatic bacteriuria occurs in 25 to 50 percent of nursing home residents, so a positive culture without urinary or systemic symptoms does not explain delirium. Accepting it ends the search for the real cause and exposes the patient to C. difficile and resistance.

checks.q: Which medication combination most commonly precipitates acute kidney injury in an older adult with a day of vomiting?
choices: Levothyroxine, calcium, and vitamin D
Metformin, aspirin, and a statin
An ACE inhibitor, a diuretic, and an NSAID
A beta blocker, a proton pump inhibitor, and a stool softener
checks.why: This triple whammy removes efferent arteriolar tone, reduces intravascular volume, and blocks the prostaglandins that maintain afferent flow, all at once. The other combinations do not attack renal perfusion from three directions simultaneously.

lessons.title: Capacity, goals of care, and the vulnerable elder
lessons.body:
## Capacity is a clinical judgment

**Capacity** is decided by the treating clinician, is specific to one decision, and can change hour to hour. **Competency** is a legal status decided by a judge. A patient may lack capacity to manage finances and retain capacity to refuse a nasogastric tube.

Four elements have to be present:

1. The patient can **communicate a choice**
2. The patient **understands** the relevant information
3. The patient **appreciates** how it applies to their own situation
4. The patient can **reason**, comparing the options against their own values

A dementia diagnosis is not by itself a loss of capacity, and neither is a decision you disagree with. The bar rises with the risk of the decision: refusing a flu shot needs less demonstrated understanding than refusing surgery for a bowel obstruction.

> **Trap:** Capacity assessments get ordered almost exclusively when a patient refuses something. If you would not have questioned capacity had they said yes, ask yourself what you are really assessing.

## The documents, and which one is an order

An **advance directive** states wishes. In New Jersey it comes in two forms, often combined: a **proxy directive** naming a health care representative, and an **instruction directive**, the living will, describing what the patient would want.

A **POLST** (Practitioner Orders for Life-Sustaining Treatment) is different in kind. It is a portable **medical order** signed by both the patient or their representative and a physician, advanced practice nurse, or physician assistant, and it travels between home, facility, and hospital. New Jersey enacted POLST in 2011.

The distinction is the point: in a resuscitation, an advance directive requires interpreting what someone meant, while a POLST is already an order. New Jersey also uses out-of-hospital DNR orders for the same reason.

When no directive exists, decisions default to next of kin by custom rather than by the statutory hierarchy many states use, so involve social work and confirm your institution's policy rather than assuming a rank order.

## Talking about goals

A goals-of-care conversation is not a request for a decision about a ventilator. It is a structured conversation:

1. Ask what they understand about their illness
2. Ask permission to share information
3. Give the news plainly, in a sentence, then stop and be quiet
4. Ask what matters most to them now and what they would not want to trade
5. Make a recommendation based on their answers, rather than presenting a menu

Avoid the false choice of asking whether they want everything done. Everyone says yes, and it does not mean what the asker thinks.

**Hospice** requires a prognosis of `6 months or less` if the disease follows its usual course, certified by two physicians, and forgoes treatment aimed at curing the terminal condition. It is a benefit, not a place, and can be revoked at any time. **Palliative care** is symptom and goals-focused care at any stage of any serious illness, alongside curative treatment.

## Elder abuse and neglect

An estimated `1 in 10` community-dwelling older adults experiences abuse, and only a small fraction is reported. Categories are physical, emotional or psychological, sexual, neglect, abandonment, and **financial exploitation**, which is among the most commonly reported.

Red flags overlap with child abuse: an injury that does not fit the history, delayed presentation, repeat visits to different facilities, unexplained dehydration or pressure injuries, pill counts that do not match, and a caregiver who answers every question and refuses to leave.

**Interview the patient alone.** That single step is the intervention.

In New Jersey, suspected abuse or neglect of a vulnerable adult in the community goes to the county **Adult Protective Services** office; for a long-term care resident it goes to the **Office of the Ombudsman for the Institutionalized Elderly**. Numbers differ by county, so use your institution's posted list.

## The nursing home transfer

A resident arriving from a facility comes with a paper packet that is often the most valuable object in the room. Get the transfer form and reason, the medication administration record, allergies, recent vitals and labs, the POLST or code status, and the direct number of the sending nurse.

Then ask the one question that reframes everything: **what is different from yesterday?** Baseline is the comparator for every finding. Confusion in someone with advanced dementia is only meaningful against what they were doing last week.

> **On shift:** Call the sending facility directly. A two-minute conversation with the nurse who knows the patient beats an hour of chart review, and it is the only way to learn that the patient walked to the dining room yesterday and could not stand this morning.
keyPoints: Capacity is clinical, decision-specific, and requires communicating a choice, understanding, appreciation, and reasoning; competency is legal.
An advance directive states wishes (proxy and instruction directive in New Jersey); a POLST is a signed, portable medical order that is followed directly.
Hospice requires a prognosis of 6 months or less and forgoes curative treatment; palliative care applies at any stage alongside any treatment.
Elder abuse affects about 1 in 10 community-dwelling older adults; interviewing the patient alone is the key step.
For a nursing home transfer, get the packet, the POLST, the sending nurse's number, and the answer to what is different from yesterday.

checks.q: A 78-year-old with mild dementia refuses admission for cellulitis. He can explain what cellulitis is, that it could spread and make him septic, that he might die, and says he would rather risk it than be away from his wife. What is the correct assessment?
choices: He lacks capacity because he has dementia
He lacks capacity because he is making a dangerous choice
He has capacity for this decision, since he communicates a choice, understands, appreciates the consequences, and reasons from his own values
Capacity cannot be assessed in dementia; seek a court order
checks.why: All four elements are demonstrated, and capacity is decision-specific rather than a global status. Neither a dementia diagnosis nor a risky choice removes capacity; a competency determination by a court is a different and slower process.

checks.q: An unresponsive patient arrives from home with a completed New Jersey POLST specifying do not resuscitate and comfort-focused care, and a living will in the same folder. What governs immediate action?
choices: The living will, because it is more detailed
The POLST, because it is a signed portable medical order that is acted on directly
Neither; full resuscitation is required until family confirms
Whichever document is dated later
checks.why: A POLST is an actionable medical order signed by a clinician and the patient or representative, while an advance directive is a statement of wishes that requires interpretation. Defaulting to full resuscitation despite a valid POLST overrides a documented decision.

checks.q: An 85-year-old arrives with dehydration, stage 3 sacral pressure injuries, and a niece who answers every question and refuses to step out. What is the most important next step?
choices: Document the findings and discharge back to the niece's care
Confront the niece about neglect
Interview the patient alone, then report suspected abuse or neglect to the appropriate New Jersey agency
Ask the niece to sign a care agreement
checks.why: Separating the patient from the caregiver is what makes disclosure possible, and the findings already meet the threshold of reasonable suspicion. Confrontation risks escalating harm at home, and discharging back into the situation without a report abandons the patient.

cards.front: At what ages should a child smile socially, sit unsupported, and walk?
cards.back: Social smile by 2 months, sits alone by about 6 to 9 months, first steps around 12 months. Referral thresholds: no smile by 3 months, not sitting by 9 months, not walking by 18 months.

cards.front: What are the language deadlines at 18 and 24 months?
cards.back: Single words by 18 months, two-word phrases by 24 months. At 2 years about 50 words and half intelligible to a stranger; at 3 years three-word sentences and 75 percent intelligible.

cards.front: Why is loss of an acquired skill always significant?
cards.back: Regression is never a normal variant. Losing words, walking, or social skills at any age requires neurologic and developmental evaluation regardless of how normal the rest of the exam appears.

cards.front: What does hand preference before 12 to 18 months suggest?
cards.back: Weakness on the non-preferred side, meaning possible hemiparesis. True handedness normally emerges after 18 months to 2 years.

cards.front: What are the normal newborn weight-loss and regain numbers?
cards.back: Up to 7 to 10 percent loss in the first week, back to birth weight by day 10 to 14, then about 20 to 30 g per day. Breastfed infants feed 8 to 12 times daily; expect 6 or more wet diapers by day 5.

cards.front: Which patterns of neonatal jaundice are always pathologic?
cards.back: Visible jaundice within the first 24 hours of life, and a direct (conjugated) bilirubin above 1 mg/dL or over 20 percent of the total, which raises biliary atresia.

cards.front: What does HEEADSSS stand for, and when is it used?
cards.back: Home, Education and employment, Eating, Activities, Drugs, Sexuality, Suicide and depression, Safety. The structured adolescent interview, done with the parent out of the room after stating confidentiality and its limits.

cards.front: Give normal heart rate and respiratory rate for a newborn, a 1-year-old, and a 10-year-old.
cards.back: Newborn HR 100 to 160, RR 30 to 60. One year HR 100 to 150, RR 24 to 40. Ten years HR 70 to 120, RR 18 to 25.

cards.front: State the pediatric hypotension thresholds by age.
cards.back: Term newborn under 60 systolic; 1 to 12 months under 70; 1 to 10 years under 70 + (2 x age in years); over 10 years under 90.

cards.front: Why is hypotension a late finding in children?
cards.back: Children compensate with tachycardia and peripheral vasoconstriction, maintaining blood pressure until roughly 30 to 40 percent of blood volume is lost. Once pressure drops, arrest is close.

cards.front: How do you estimate weight in a child aged 1 to 10 without a scale?
cards.back: (age in years x 2) + 8 = kilograms. Better is a length-based color-coded resuscitation tape, which also gives doses and equipment sizes but underestimates in obese children.

cards.front: What are the three sides of the pediatric assessment triangle?
cards.back: Appearance (TICLS: tone, interactiveness, consolability, look or gaze, speech or cry), work of breathing, and circulation to skin. Done from the doorway in under 30 seconds.

cards.front: Abnormal appearance with normal breathing and normal circulation suggests what?
cards.back: A primary brain or metabolic problem: hypoglycemia, intoxication, postictal state, head injury, or sepsis affecting the brain. Check a glucose immediately.

cards.front: What does grunting mean in an infant?
cards.back: The infant is exhaling against a partly closed glottis to create their own positive end-expiratory pressure. It signals impending respiratory failure, not a mild illness.

cards.front: What temperature defines fever in an infant, and by which route?
cards.back: A rectal temperature of 38.0 C (100.4 F) or higher. Rectal is the standard under 3 years; axillary, temporal, and tympanic readings are screening only in infants.

cards.front: What is the workup and disposition for a febrile infant under 28 days?
cards.back: CBC, blood culture, catheterized urinalysis and culture, lumbar puncture with CSF culture, consider HSV testing; empiric antibiotics and admission. There is no well-appearing exception.

cards.front: Which inflammatory markers risk-stratify a febrile infant 29 to 60 days old?
cards.back: Procalcitonin above 0.5 ng/mL, C-reactive protein above 20 mg/L, absolute neutrophil count above about 4,000 to 5,200 per microliter, or temperature above 38.5 C.

cards.front: Why must an infant urine culture be catheterized rather than bagged?
cards.back: Bag specimens have contamination rates high enough that a positive culture is uninterpretable. A negative bag urinalysis can rule out, but any positive must be recollected by catheter or suprapubic aspiration.

cards.front: How does meningitis present in an infant under 12 months?
cards.back: Bulging fontanelle, paradoxical irritability (worse when held), poor feeding, high-pitched cry, and temperature instability including hypothermia. Kernig and Brudzinski signs are unreliable at this age.

cards.front: Define a simple versus complex febrile seizure.
cards.back: Simple: generalized, under 15 minutes, once in 24 hours, ages 6 months to 5 years with fever and no CNS infection. Complex: focal, over 15 minutes, or recurrent within 24 hours.

cards.front: What is the recurrence and epilepsy risk after a simple febrile seizure?
cards.back: Recurrence about 30 to 35 percent; later epilepsy about 1 to 2 percent, barely above the population baseline. No routine LP, imaging, or EEG in a well, immunized child over 12 months.

cards.front: What is the evidence-based treatment of bronchiolitis?
cards.back: Nasal suctioning, hydration, and oxygen for hypoxia. Not recommended: routine bronchodilators, corticosteroids, antibiotics, or chest radiographs. Watch for apnea in infants under 2 months and in preterm infants.

cards.front: What is the dexamethasone dose in croup, and who gets it?
cards.back: 0.6 mg/kg as a single PO, IM, or IV dose, given for every severity including mild croup, because it shortens symptoms and reduces return visits.

cards.front: When is nebulized epinephrine given in croup, and what must follow?
cards.back: For stridor at rest (moderate or severe). Observe 2 to 4 hours afterward, because the effect wears off before the subglottic edema does and rebound stridor can occur.

cards.front: What is the Westley croup score range and severity cutoffs?
cards.back: 0 to 17, scoring consciousness, cyanosis, stridor, air entry, and retractions. Mild 2 or less, moderate 3 to 5, severe 6 to 11, impending respiratory failure 12 or more.

cards.front: Give the first-hour pediatric asthma regimen with doses.
cards.back: Albuterol 2.5 mg nebulized under 20 kg or 5 mg at 20 kg and above; ipratropium 0.5 mg for moderate to severe, up to 3 doses; systemic steroid within 1 hour (prednisolone 1 to 2 mg/kg, max 60 mg, or dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg).

cards.front: What is the magnesium dose for severe pediatric asthma, and what does a silent chest mean?
cards.back: Magnesium sulfate 25 to 50 mg/kg IV, maximum 2 g. A silent chest means air movement has stopped; disappearance of wheeze without clinical improvement is a preterminal sign.

cards.front: What is the most sensitive sign of pediatric pneumonia, and the WHO rate cutoffs?
cards.back: Tachypnea. Respiratory rate over 60 under 2 months, over 50 from 2 to 12 months, over 40 from 1 to 5 years. First-line outpatient therapy is amoxicillin about 90 mg/kg/day.

cards.front: How does pertussis present in an infant under 1 year?
cards.back: Apnea, cyanosis, and coughing spells with feeding, often without a whoop. Highest mortality age group. Treat with azithromycin; maternal Tdap at 27 to 36 weeks is the main protection.

cards.front: How do you recognize a pediatric airway foreign body, and why is a normal x-ray unhelpful?
cards.back: Abrupt onset, focal wheeze, unilateral decreased breath sounds, usually right mainstem. Most aspirated objects are radiolucent, so a normal film does not exclude it; rigid bronchoscopy is diagnostic and therapeutic.

cards.front: Give the clinical estimates for mild, moderate, and severe pediatric dehydration.
cards.back: Mild about 3 to 5 percent, normal vitals. Moderate about 6 to 9 percent: dry mucosa, tachycardia, refill 2 to 3 s, sunken eyes. Severe 10 percent or more: lethargy, refill over 3 s, anuria; hypotension is late.

cards.front: What are the oral rehydration volumes and technique?
